The Ñandeva, also called Avá Guaraní or Chiripá, are a Guaraní people of the forests between the Paraná and Paraguay rivers, in eastern Paraguay and the Brazilian states of Paraná and Mato Grosso do Sul. Tekohá is the Guaraní word for their homeland, "the place where we live as we are".

They farmed maize and manioc in forest clearings, hunted and fished, and moved villages in search of good land. Their kin include the Mbyá and the Kaiowá.

In the early 1600s Jesuit priests gathered many Guaraní into the Jesuit reductions. Slave raiders from São Paulo, the bandeirantes, attacked these towns around 1630. In modern times ranches and the Itaipu Dam, which flooded part of the Paraná valley in 1982, pushed many Avá Guaraní off their land in Paraguay and Brazil.
